faq.q: Why is potassium replacement delayed in DKA?

faq.a: It can worsen hyperglycaemia and delay correction of acidosis.
faq.q: What is the danger of giving dextrose before insulin?

faq.a: Use capillary glucose, urine ketones and clinical signs to guide treatment; start insulin and fluids anyway.
faq.q: How to manage a patient when serum bicarbonate is unavailable?

exam: A 28‑year‑old with type 1 DM presents with vomiting and confusion. Blood glucose is 480 mg/dL. What is the next best step? — Start insulin infusion after initial fluid resuscitation; check electrolytes and ketones.
A 45‑year‑old with type 2 DM is found unconscious. Serum osmolality is 330 mOsm/kg. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state; treat with fluids and insulin.
Why is potassium monitoring essential in DKA? — Insulin shifts potassium intracellularly; low serum potassium can cause arrhythmias.
A patient with DKA has serum potassium 2.8 mmol/L. What is the safest way to correct it? — Replace potassium only after insulin started and serum >3.3 mmol/L.
What complication is most feared in children with DKA? — Cerebral oedema; monitor for headache, vomiting, seizures.
A patient with suspected DKA has a negative urine ketone test. What should you do? — Repeat test or use serum β‑hydroxybutyrate; treat as DKA if clinical picture fits.
Why is dextrose avoided until glucose <200 mg/dL in DKA? — To prevent rebound hyperglycaemia and delay acidosis correction.
What is the key difference between DKA and HHS? — DKA has ketosis and acidosis; HHS has extreme hyperosmolality without significant acidosis.
ai.title: Hyperglycaemic Emergencies
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Acute metabolic derangements from uncontrolled diabetes presenting with life‑threatening complications. Rapid recognition, diagnosis and management are essential, especially where investigations are limited.

b: DKA: glucose >250 mg/dL, pH <7.3, bicarbonate <18 mmol/L, ketones positive
HHS: glucose >600 mg/dL, serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, pH >7.3, bicarbonate >18 mmol/L
sections.p: Hyperglycaemic emergencies are acute, severe metabolic disturbances in diabetes characterised by marked hyperglycaemia and either ketoacidosis or hyperosmolarity.
